### Power associativity gives exponent laws

**Remember:** Each single element lives in its own associative world.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A05 (Power-associative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** An algebra is power-associative if the subalgebra generated by each single element is associative, so every bracketing of xⁿ gives the same element. Checking only (xx)x = x(xx) is weaker.

**Problem.** In a power-associative algebra, xᵐxⁿ = xᵐ⁺ⁿ for all positive integers m and n.

**How the definition helps.** All powers of x lie in an associative subalgebra, where regrouping gives xᵐxⁿ = xᵐ⁺ⁿ (our own). The third-power test alone fails in the commutative algebra with basis e,f,g, ee = f, ff = g and all other basis products zero. Commutativity gives (xx)x = x(xx), but (ee)(ee) = g while e(e(ee)) = 0 (our own).

**nLab:** [power-associative algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/power-associative+algebra). It says: “it may be that all possible ways of parenthesizing the expression for xⁿ are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating brackets exclude a characteristic two counterexample

**Remember:** Alternation implies anticommutativity even when 2 is zero.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 17B50. arXiv math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lie bracket on a vector space is bilinear, alternating (\[x,x\] = 0 for every x, not merely \[x,y\] = −\[y,x\]), and satisfies the Jacobi identity \[x,\[y,z\]\] + \[y,\[z,x\]\] + \[z,\[x,y\]\] = 0.

**Problem.** Every Lie bracket is anticommutative. In characteristic two, anticommutativity and the Jacobi identity do not suffice for a Lie bracket.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding \[x+y,x+y\] = 0 gives \[x,y\] = −\[y,x\] (our own). The converse fails in characteristic two: over the two-element field with basis e,f, set \[e,e\] = f and all other basis brackets zero. This bracket is symmetric, hence anticommutative, and all nested brackets vanish, so Jacobi holds, but \[e,e\] ≠ 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra). It says: “If the field does not have characteristic 2, then anticommutativity implies the alternating property, since it implies \[x,x\]=−\[x,x\].”

**Paper or page:** [Lie Algebra is Anticommutative](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Lie_Algebra_is_Anticommutative). It says: “Let L be a Lie algebra. Then L is anticommutative:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Jacobi as a product rule gives the adjoint representation

**Remember:** Jacobi says ad turns brackets into commutators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B01 (Identities, free Lie (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Lie bracket is bilinear and alternating and obeys the product rule \[x,\[a,b\]\] = \[\[x,a\],b\] + \[a,\[x,b\]\], so each adₓ = \[x,−\] is a derivation.

**Problem.** The map x ↦ adₓ preserves brackets, using the commutator AB − BA as the bracket of operators.

**How the definition helps.** Move the last term left: \[x,\[a,b\]\] − \[a,\[x,b\]\] = \[\[x,a\],b\], which reads (adₓ adₐ − adₐ adₓ)(b) = ad\_\[x,a\](b) (our own). That is exactly the claim (our own). For an alternating bracket this product rule is equivalent to the cyclic Jacobi identity (our own).

**nLab:** [Jacobi identity](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Jacobi+identity). It says: “If the bracket \[−,−\] is skew-symmetric the Jacobi identity for all triples is equivalent to the Leibniz identity that for all x,a,b, the linear map adₓ = \[x,−\] : 𝔤 → 𝔤 is a derivation”

**Wikipedia:** [Adjoint representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adjoint_representation). It says: “This last identity says that ad is a Lie algebra homomorphism; i.e., a linear mapping that takes brackets to brackets.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Ruling out abelian ideals makes the adjoint representation faithful

**Remember:** The centre is an abelian ideal, so it vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A finite-dimensional Lie algebra 𝔤 is semisimple if it has no nonzero abelian ideal, that is, no nonzero subspace I with \[𝔤,I\] ⊆ I and \[I,I\] = 0.

**Problem.** For a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 in characteristic zero, the adjoint representation x ↦ \[x,−\] is injective.

**How the definition helps.** The kernel of x ↦ \[x,−\] is the centre, the elements that bracket to zero with everything. The centre is an abelian ideal, so semisimplicity forces it to be zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “The center of a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 is trivial (since the center is an abelian ideal). In other words, the adjoint representation ad is injective.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Killing squares gives Lie quotients

**Remember:** Kill the squares to get a Lie bracket in every characteristic.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A32 (Leibniz algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A left Leibniz algebra has a bilinear bracket for which each \[x,−\] obeys the product rule \[x,\[y,z\]\] = \[\[x,y\],z\] + \[y,\[x,z\]\]. Its Lie quotient divides out the span of all squares \[x,x\], so the bracket becomes alternating.

**Problem.** Every bracket-preserving linear map from a left Leibniz algebra to a Lie algebra factors uniquely through its Lie quotient.

**How the definition helps.** A map to a Lie algebra sends every square to zero, so it kills their span and factors uniquely through the quotient (our own). The span is an ideal: the rule gives \[\[x,x\],y\] = 0, and \[y,\[x,x\]\] = \[u,x\] + \[x,u\] with u = \[y,x\], a combination of squares. In the quotient the bracket alternates, so the product rule becomes Jacobi.

**nLab:** [Leibniz algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Leibniz+algebra). It says: “the maximal Lie algebra quotient”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Louis Loday and Teimuraz Pirashvili. Universal enveloping algebras of Leibniz algebras and (co)homology (1993).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01445099)

### Anisotropic composition norms give division

**Remember:** A product of nonzero norms cannot be zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17A75 (Composition algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A unital composition algebra over a field has an identity and a nondegenerate quadratic norm N with N(xy) = N(x)N(y). The norm is anisotropic if only zero has norm zero.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional composition algebra with anisotropic norm, multiplication by any nonzero element is invertible on both sides.

**How the definition helps.** If x and y are nonzero, then N(xy) = N(x)N(y) ≠ 0, so xy ≠ 0 (our own). Left and right multiplication by a nonzero element are therefore injective, hence invertible in finite dimension. Without anisotropy this fails: in 2×2 matrices with the determinant as norm, the diagonal matrices diag(1,0) and diag(0,1) multiply to zero (our own).

**nLab:** [composition algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/composition+algebra). It says: “A fundamental dichotomy is whether or not the composition algebra has zero divisors, i.e., elements v such that N(v) = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Cartan subalgebras as maximal toral makes the rank well defined

**Remember:** A Cartan subalgebra is nilpotent and equals its own normalizer.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B05 (Structure theory for Lie algebras and superalgebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Cartan subalgebra of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is a nilpotent subalgebra C that equals its own normalizer, the set of x with \[x,C\] ⊆ C.

**Problem.** Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic 0, all Cartan subalgebras of a finite-dimensional Lie algebra are conjugate under automorphisms. So their common dimension, the rank, is an invariant.

**How the definition helps.** The Cartan conjugacy theorem applies to exactly these subalgebras over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, and conjugate subalgebras have equal dimension (our own). Maximal abelian subalgebras would not work. In sl₂ₙ(ℂ) for n ≥ 2, the matrices supported in the upper right n×n block commute and span dimension n², more than the rank 2n − 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cartan subalgebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartan_subalgebra). It says: “The dimension of a Cartan subalgebra is not in general the maximal dimension of an abelian subalgebra, even for complex simple Lie algebras.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Invariant pairings identify the center

**Remember:** Move the bracket across the pairing to detect central elements.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B05 (Structure theory for Lie algebras and superalgebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A metric Lie algebra has a nondegenerate symmetric bilinear form B that is invariant, B(\[x,y\],z) = B(x,\[y,z\]), so a bracket can move across the form. An arbitrary inner product need not obey this rule.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional metric Lie algebra, the center is the orthogonal complement of the span of all brackets.

**How the definition helps.** Invariance gives B(z,\[x,y\]) = B(\[z,x\],y), so z is orthogonal to all brackets exactly when each \[z,x\] pairs to zero with everything (our own). Nondegeneracy turns this into \[z,x\] = 0 for every x (our own). Without invariance it fails: on the real Heisenberg algebra with orthonormal basis x,y,z and \[x,y\] = z, the brackets span the z-axis and the centre is also the z-axis, not the plane perpendicular to it (our own).

**nLab:** [metric Lie algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/metric+Lie+algebra). It says: “is symmetric and invariant under the adjoint action, hence is an invariant polynomial on 𝔤”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fundamental weights make integral weights the integer combinations of a basis

**Remember:** Coroots test integrality; fundamental weights are their dual basis.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)), 17B22. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A weight λ is algebraically integral if its pairing (λ,α∨) with every coroot α∨ = 2α/(α,α) is an integer. The fundamental weights are the basis dual to the simple coroots, so the i-th coefficient of λ is (λ,αᵢ∨).

**Problem.** A weight is algebraically integral if and only if it is an integer combination of the fundamental weights. It is dominant integral, with (λ,α∨) ≥ 0 for every positive root α, exactly when these integers are all nonnegative.

**How the definition helps.** By duality, the coefficients of λ are its pairings with the simple coroots. Every positive coroot is a nonnegative integer combination of simple coroots, so integral and nonnegative simple pairings give the same for all coroots (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weight (representation theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weight_%28representation_theory%29), [Root system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_system). It says: “An element λ is then algebraically integral if and only if it is an integral combination of the fundamental weights.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Induction gives Verma modules their universal property

**Remember:** Induction turns a choice of highest weight vector into a module map.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Verma module M(λ) = U(𝔤) ⊗ ℂλ, with the tensor product over U(𝔟), is the 𝔤-module freely generated by one vector of weight λ killed by the positive root spaces. Here 𝔟 is a Borel subalgebra of a complex semisimple 𝔤, the Cartan 𝔥 plus the positive root spaces, acting on the line ℂλ by λ on 𝔥 and by zero elsewhere.

**Problem.** Every 𝔤-module generated by a vector of weight λ killed by the positive root spaces is a quotient of M(λ).

**How the definition helps.** By induction, a 𝔤-map from M(λ) to V is the same as a choice of weight-λ vector in V killed by the positive root spaces (our own). If that vector generates V, the map is surjective.

**nLab:** [Verma module](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Verma+module). It says: “Given a semisimple Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field F with Borel subalgebra 𝔟 ⊂ 𝔤 a Verma module is the induced module”

**Wikipedia:** [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module). It says: “If V is any representation generated by a highest weight vector of weight λ, there is a surjective 𝔤-homomorphism W\_\\lambda\\to V.”

**Sources:**

- [D.-N. Verma, Structure of certain induced representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 74 (1968) 160–167](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9904-1968-11921-4)

### Verma modules give an irreducible module of every highest weight

**Remember:** Build the largest module of weight λ first, then cut it down.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B10 (Representations of Lie algebras and Lie superalgebras, algebraic theory (weights)). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Verma module M(λ) = U(𝔤) ⊗ ℂλ, with the tensor product over U(𝔟), is the module freely generated by one vector of weight λ killed by the positive root spaces. Here 𝔟 is a Borel subalgebra of a complex semisimple 𝔤 with Cartan subalgebra 𝔥, and λ ∈ 𝔥\*.

**Problem.** For every linear form λ on 𝔥, the Verma module of weight λ has a unique irreducible quotient. So there is exactly one irreducible module of highest weight λ, up to isomorphism.

**How the definition helps.** Every module of highest weight λ is a quotient of M(λ), and by the Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt theorem the λ-weight space of M(λ) is one line (our own). A submodule is proper exactly when it misses that line, so the sum of all proper submodules is still proper (our own). This sum is the unique maximal submodule, so the irreducible quotient is unique (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Verma module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Verma_module), [Theorem of the highest weight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theorem_of_the_highest_weight). It says: “In any case, the Verma module gives—for any λ, not necessarily dominant or integral—a representation with highest weight λ. The price we pay for this relatively simple construction is that Wλ is always infinite dimensional.”

**Sources:**

- [Verma, D.-N. (1968). Structure of certain induced representations of complex semisimple Lie algebras. Bulletin of the AMS 74, 160–167.](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1968-11921-4)
- [Bernshtein, I. N., Gel'fand, I. M., Gel'fand, S. I. (1971). Structure of representations generated by vectors of highest weight. Functional Analysis and Its Applications 5, 1–8.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01075841)

### Abelian Lie algebras are not simple, so semisimple means no abelian ideals

**Remember:** Simple means no proper ideals and not abelian, so lines are excluded.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A simple Lie algebra is a non-abelian Lie algebra whose only ideals are 0 and itself. A semisimple Lie algebra is a direct sum of simple ones, so no summand is the abelian line.

**Problem.** A finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero is a direct sum of simple algebras exactly when it has no nonzero abelian ideal. Equivalently, its Killing form (x,y) ↦ tr(adₓ adᵧ) is nondegenerate.

**How the definition helps.** Requiring nonabelian factors removes the one-dimensional algebra, which has no proper nonzero ideal but is an abelian ideal with zero Killing form (our own). The structure theorem equates direct sums of simples with having no nonzero solvable ideal, and a nonzero solvable ideal ends its derived series in a nonzero abelian ideal. Cartan’s criterion gives the Killing form equivalence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Simple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Lie_algebra), [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “In algebra, a simple Lie algebra is a Lie algebra that is non-abelian and contains no nonzero proper ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Chevalley's integral basis builds the finite groups of Lie type uniformly

**Remember:** Integer structure constants let every simple Lie algebra make finite groups.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 20G40. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Chevalley basis of a complex simple Lie algebra consists of simple coroots hᵢ and root vectors eα with \[eα,e₋α\] = hα and \[eα,eβ\] = ±(p+1)eα₊β when α+β is a root. Here p is the largest j ≥ 0 with β − jα a root, so all structure constants are integers.

**Problem.** For each complex simple Lie algebra and finite field, the adjoint Chevalley construction gives a finite group, simple apart from the small-field exceptions. This construction includes the classical untwisted types and the exceptional types E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄ and G₂.

**How the definition helps.** Integer structure constants make the divided powers eαⁿ/n! act integrally, so the root group elements exp(t eα) make sense over every finite field (our own). They generate the finite adjoint Chevalley group. Chevalley’s simplicity theorem gives simplicity apart from the small-field exceptions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Group of Lie type](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Lie_type). It says: “Chevalley constructed a Chevalley basis (a sort of integral form but over finite fields) for all the complex simple Lie algebras”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley, Sur certains groupes simples, Tôhoku Mathematical Journal 7 (1955) 14–66](https://doi.org/10.2748/tmj/1178245104)

### Defining Lie algebras by Serre relations lifts diagram symmetries

**Remember:** A symmetry of the relations permutes the generators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras). arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Lie algebra of a finite-type Cartan matrix A has generators eᵢ, fᵢ, hᵢ and Chevalley–Serre relations that use the indices only through the entries Aᵢⱼ (our own). A diagram automorphism is a permutation π of the indices with A\_π(i)π(j) = Aᵢⱼ for every pair i,j.

**Problem.** Every permutation of the indices that preserves the Cartan matrix gives an automorphism of the Lie algebra. The automorphism permutes the generators eᵢ, fᵢ and hᵢ in the same way.

**How the definition helps.** Such a permutation sends every relation to a relation, so it induces a homomorphism of the Lie algebra (our own). The inverse permutation induces its inverse.

**nLab:** [Cartan matrix](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Cartan+matrix). It says: “In fact, 𝔤 is presented by generators eᵢ, fᵢ, hᵢ and the relations”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Starting each classical family at the right rank makes the list non-redundant

**Remember:** Start B at two, C at three, D at four, and nothing repeats.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B20 (Simple, semisimple, reductive (super)algebras), 17B22. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The classical families of complex simple Lie algebras are Aₙ = slₙ₊₁, Bₙ = so₂ₙ₊₁, Cₙ = sp₂ₙ and Dₙ = so₂ₙ, indexed by the rank n. They start at ranks 1, 2, 3 and 4, because lower ranks repeat another entry or are not simple.

**Problem.** Up to isomorphism, each finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra occurs exactly once among the four families in these ranges and the five exceptional algebras. Every entry is simple.

**How the definition helps.** Below the starting ranks the families overlap or fail to be simple: B₁ ≅ A₁, C₂ ≅ B₂, D₃ ≅ A₃, and D₂ splits into two simple factors (our own). The classification by Dynkin diagrams gives completeness and uniqueness (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Semisimple Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semisimple_Lie_algebra). It says: “The enumeration of the four families is non-redundant and consists only of simple algebras if n ≥ 1 for Aₙ, n ≥ 2 for Bₙ, n ≥ 3 for Cₙ, and n ≥ 4 for Dₙ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced crystallographic root systems are exactly those that Dynkin diagrams classify

**Remember:** Integer Cartan numbers and no doubled roots leave only A to G.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B22 (Root systems), 17B20. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A root system is a finite spanning set of nonzero Euclidean vectors, closed under the reflection perpendicular to each root. It is crystallographic if every 2(α,β)/(α,α) is an integer, and reduced if the only roots proportional to a root α are ±α.

**Problem.** Every irreducible reduced crystallographic root system has type Aₙ, Bₙ, Cₙ, Dₙ, E₆, E₇, E₈, F₄ or G₂. These are exactly the root systems of finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebras.

**How the definition helps.** Integrality excludes systems such as the decagonal I₂(5), and reducedness excludes BCₙ, which contains both e₁ and 2e₁ (our own). Dynkin diagram classification gives the list, and the complex simple Lie algebras realize every type (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Root system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Root_system). It says: “Other authors omit condition 2; then they call root systems satisfying condition 2 reduced. In this article, all root systems are assumed to be reduced and crystallographic.”

**Sources:**

- [Killing, W. (1888). Die Zusammensetzung der stetigen endlichen Transformationsgruppen. Mathematische Annalen 33, 1–48.](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01444109)

### Root reflections make the Weyl group visibly finite

**Remember:** Root reflections permute a finite spanning set.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B22 (Root systems), 20F55. arXiv math.RT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Weyl group of a root system Φ is the group generated by the reflections perpendicular to the roots. Each such reflection permutes the finite set Φ, which spans the space.

**Problem.** The Weyl group of a root system is finite.

**How the definition helps.** Every element of the Weyl group permutes Φ, and an element fixing every root fixes their span, so it is the identity (our own). The Weyl group therefore embeds in the finite group of permutations of Φ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weyl group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_group). It says: “By the definition of a root system, each s\_\\alpha preserves Φ, from which it follows that W is a finite group.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining enveloping algebras as left adjoints makes them preserve free products

**Remember:** Left adjoints preserve coproducts, and free products are coproducts.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 18A40. arXiv math.RA, math.CT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The enveloping algebra U(𝔤) is the unital associative algebra through which every Lie map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, extends uniquely as a unital algebra map U(𝔤) → A. So U is left adjoint to the functor that views an associative algebra as a Lie algebra.

**Problem.** The enveloping algebra of a free product of Lie algebras is the free product of their enveloping algebras. Free products are the coproducts in both categories.

**How the definition helps.** The universal property makes U a left adjoint, and every left adjoint preserves coproducts. Free products are the coproducts of Lie algebras and of unital associative algebras (our own).

**nLab:** [universal enveloping algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+enveloping+algebra). It says: “which is the left adjoint to the forgetful functor”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining enveloping algebras universally makes direct sums give tensor products

**Remember:** Commuting Lie summands become commuting tensor factors.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The enveloping algebra U(𝔤) is the unital associative algebra through which every Lie map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, extends uniquely as a unital algebra map. In a direct sum 𝔤 ⊕ 𝔥, the two summands bracket to zero with each other.

**Problem.** Over a field, the enveloping algebra of a direct sum 𝔤 ⊕ 𝔥 of Lie algebras is the tensor product U(𝔤) ⊗ U(𝔥).

**How the definition helps.** An algebra map from either side to A amounts to Lie maps from 𝔤 and 𝔥 into A with commuting images (our own). For U(𝔤 ⊕ 𝔥) this holds because the summands bracket to zero, and for U(𝔤) ⊗ U(𝔥) by the universal property of the tensor product (our own). Both algebras have the same maps out, so they are isomorphic (our own).

**nLab:** [universal enveloping algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+enveloping+algebra). It says: “in the category of enveloping algebras of L, which implies that it is unique up to an isomorphism if it exists.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Free Lie algebras yield tensor algebras

**Remember:** Two extension rules in a row give the free associative algebra.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B01. arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Both objects are defined by an extension rule. Every map from a set X to a Lie algebra extends uniquely to a Lie map out of the free Lie algebra on X, and every Lie map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, extends uniquely to a unital algebra map out of U(𝔤).

**Problem.** The enveloping algebra of the free Lie algebra on a set is the free unital associative algebra on that set.

**How the definition helps.** Composing the two rules, every map from X to an associative algebra extends uniquely to a unital algebra map out of U of the free Lie algebra on X (our own). That is the defining property of the free associative algebra on X.

**Wikipedia:** [Free Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Lie_algebra). It says: “The universal enveloping algebra of a free Lie algebra on a set X is the free associative algebra generated by X.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Restricted enveloping algebras enforce powers

**Remember:** Put power preservation in the quotient, and every module respects it.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A restricted Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field of characteristic p &gt; 0 has a power map P. Its restricted enveloping algebra is U(𝔤) modulo the relations xᵖ = P(x) for all x in 𝔤, and a restricted representation is a representation ρ with ρ(P(x)) = ρ(x)ᵖ.

**Problem.** Modules over the restricted enveloping algebra are exactly the restricted representations.

**How the definition helps.** A Lie representation, that is a U(𝔤)-module, factors through the quotient exactly when each relation xᵖ − P(x) acts as zero, which is the restricted condition (our own). Ordinary representations can fail this. On a one-dimensional algebra with zero power map, let the basis element act as the identity, whose pth power is not zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Restricted Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restricted_Lie_algebra). It says: “Restricted representations of 𝔤 are equivalent to modules over the restricted enveloping algebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Casimir tensor gives a basis-free central element

**Remember:** The identity map, multiplied out, chooses no basis and commutes.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Casimir element of a finite-dimensional complex Lie algebra 𝔤 is the identity map of 𝔤, made a tensor in 𝔤 ⊗ 𝔤 by an invariant nondegenerate symmetric form B, then multiplied out in U(𝔤) (our own). In a basis xᵢ with B-dual basis xⁱ, it is ∑ xᵢxⁱ.

**Problem.** The resulting Casimir element is independent of the basis and commutes with every element of U(𝔤).

**How the definition helps.** The identity map involves no basis and commutes with every adjoint operator (our own). Invariance of B carries this to the tensor, and multiplication turns the adjoint action into commutators (our own). So the element commutes with each generator of U(𝔤), hence with all of U(𝔤) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Casimir element](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casimir_element). It says: “Although the definition relies on a choice of basis for the Lie algebra, it is easy to show that Ω is independent of this choice.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Casimir and B. L. van der Waerden, Algebraischer Beweis der vollständigen Reduzibilität der Darstellungen halbeinfacher Liescher Gruppen, Mathematische Annalen 111 (1935) 1–12](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01472196)

### The enveloping algebra turns the diagonal into a coproduct

**Remember:** Extend the diagonal by the unique algebra map on the enveloping algebra.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 16T05. arXiv math.RA, math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The enveloping algebra U(𝔤) is the unital associative algebra through which every Lie map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, extends uniquely as a unital algebra map. The map x ↦ x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x into U(𝔤) ⊗ U(𝔤) is such a Lie map (our own).

**Problem.** U(𝔤) is a Hopf algebra with coproduct x ↦ x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x, counit x ↦ 0 and antipode x ↦ −x for x in 𝔤.

**How the definition helps.** Extending x ↦ x ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ x, x ↦ 0 and x ↦ −x into the opposite algebra gives the coproduct, counit and antipode; the first is U applied to the diagonal (our own). Coassociativity and the counit laws hold on generators, so they hold everywhere by uniqueness (our own). The antipode identities extend from generators to products because the antipode reverses multiplication (our own).

**nLab:** [universal enveloping algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+enveloping+algebra). It says: “The coproduct Δ: U(L) → U(L × L) ≅ U(L) ⊗ U(L) is induced by the diagonal map L → L × L”

**Sources:**

- [J. W. Milnor and J. C. Moore, On the structure of Hopf algebras, Annals of Mathematics 81 (1965) 211–264](https://doi.org/10.2307/1970615)

### The universal enveloping algebra makes Lie algebra representations into modules

**Remember:** A Lie action extends uniquely from brackets to associative products.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B35 (Universal enveloping (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The enveloping algebra U(𝔤) is the unital associative algebra through which every Lie map from 𝔤 to an associative algebra A, with bracket ab − ba, extends uniquely as a unital algebra map. A representation of 𝔤 on V is such a Lie map into A = End(V).

**Problem.** Representations of 𝔤 on V correspond to U(𝔤)-module structures on V. Central elements, including any Casimir element, act on every representation and act by scalars on finite-dimensional irreducible complex representations.

**How the definition helps.** Apply the universal property to A = End(V) to extend each representation uniquely to a U(𝔤)-module. A central element then acts by a module endomorphism, so Schur’s lemma makes it a scalar on finite-dimensional irreducible complex modules (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Universal enveloping algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_enveloping_algebra). It says: “The universal property of the enveloping algebra immediately implies that every representation of 𝔤 acting on a vector space V extends uniquely to a representation of U(𝔤).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Lie algebras by dual-number points makes Lie commute with kernels

**Remember:** A tangent vector of a kernel is a tangent vector killed by the map.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B45 (Lie algebras of linear algebraic groups), 14L15. arXiv math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a group scheme G over a field k, Lie(G) is the set of points of G over the dual numbers k\[t\]/(t²) that reduce to the identity at t = 0.

**Problem.** Take a map of affine group schemes G → H over a field. The Lie algebra of its kernel is the kernel of the map of Lie algebras. Here the kernel is the scheme kernel, which may have nilpotent functions.

**How the definition helps.** A point of the Lie algebra of the kernel is a point of G(k\[t\]/(t²)) that reduces to the identity and maps to the identity of H. These are exactly the points of Lie(G) that map to zero in Lie(H) (our own).

**nLab:** [affine group scheme](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/affine+group+scheme). It says: “This Lie algebra is also isomorphic to the Lie algebra of k-linear k-valued derivations of 𝒪(X).”

**Sources:**

- [J. S. Milne, Algebraic Groups, version 2.00 (2015), §12c, 12.12, and §12e](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/iAG200.pdf)

### Dual numbers expose derivations in the automorphism group

**Remember:** The coefficient of ε is the product rule.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B45 (Lie algebras of linear algebraic groups), 17B40. arXiv math.AG, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a group scheme G over k, Lie(G) consists of the points over the dual numbers k\[ε\]/(ε²) that reduce to the identity at ε = 0. For the automorphism group of an algebra A, these are the automorphisms 1 + εD of A\[ε\] with D linear.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite-dimensional unital associative k-algebra. The Lie algebra of its automorphism group scheme is the Lie algebra of derivations of A, the linear maps D with D(xy) = D(x)y + xD(y), under the commutator bracket.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding (1+εD)(xy) = (1+εD)(x)·(1+εD)(y) modulo ε² gives exactly D(xy) = D(x)y + xD(y). Conversely each derivation gives an automorphism with inverse 1 − εD (our own). The group commutator in two independent square-zero parameters yields the bracket DE − ED (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra). It says: “Indeed, writing out the condition that (1+εD)(xy) ≡ (1+εD)(x)·(1+εD)(y) (mod ε²) (where 1 denotes the identity map on A) gives exactly the definition of D being a derivation.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Invariant derivations give Lie algebras a pth power

**Remember:** All the middle binomial coefficients vanish in characteristic p.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras), 14L15, 17B45. arXiv math.RA, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an affine group scheme over k with coordinate algebra A and coproduct Δ, Lie(G) is the space of left-invariant derivations of A, the k-linear maps D with D(fg) = D(f)g + fD(g) and ΔD = (id ⊗ D)Δ. These are operators on A, so powers such as Dᵖ make sense.

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic p &gt; 0, the Lie algebra of an affine group scheme has a natural restricted Lie algebra structure. This adds a pth power operation with the laws of pth powers in an associative algebra.

**How the definition helps.** By the product rule, Dᵖ(fg) is the sum over i of (p choose i)Dⁱ(f)Dᵖ⁻ⁱ(g), and the middle coefficients vanish in characteristic p, so Dᵖ is a derivation (our own). Dᵖ is still left-invariant, and the restricted identities hold because they hold for powers in the associative algebra Endₖ(A) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Restricted Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restricted_Lie_algebra). It says: “When k has characteristic p&gt;0, then iterating a derivation p times yields a derivation, and this makes Derₖ(A) into a restricted Lie algebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Zero center makes powers unique

**Remember:** Equal adjoint powers differ by a central element, which must vanish.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B50 (Modular Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Lie algebra 𝔤 has zero center when only 0 brackets to zero with every element. In characteristic p &gt; 0, a restricted power map P must satisfy ad(P(x)) = ad(x)ᵖ, so ad fixes P(x) up to a central element (our own).

**Problem.** A Lie algebra with zero center has at most one restricted power map.

**How the definition helps.** Two power maps give values for P(x) with the same adjoint operator ad(x)ᵖ, so their difference is central and hence zero (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Restricted Lie algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restricted_Lie_algebra). It says: “their difference is a p-linear function from 𝔤 to the center 𝔷(𝔤).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### As codifferentials, L∞-algebras turn all higher Jacobi identities into D² = 0

**Remember:** All brackets form one coderivation D; Jacobi says D² = 0.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 17B55 (Homological methods in Lie (super)algebras), 18M70. arXiv math.QA, math.AT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An uncurved L∞ structure on a graded vector space 𝔤 over a field of characteristic zero is a single degree −1 coderivation D with D² = 0. It acts on the reduced cofree conilpotent cocommutative coalgebra on the suspension of 𝔤, and its components in each arity are the brackets.

**Problem.** A family of graded skew brackets of the prescribed degrees satisfies the higher Jacobi identities exactly when its associated coderivation squares to zero. L∞ morphisms are differential graded coalgebra maps between the corresponding coalgebras.

**How the definition helps.** By cofreeness, the suspended brackets determine a unique coderivation D (our own). Its square D² is again a coderivation, so its projections to the cogenerators determine it (our own). In each arity that projection is the corresponding higher Jacobi identity (our own).

**nLab:** [L-infinity-algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/L-infinity-algebra). It says: “The higher Jacobi identity is equivalently the condition that D² = 0.”

**Sources:**

- [Tom Lada, Jim Stasheff, Introduction to sh Lie algebras for physicists, Int. J. Theor. Phys. 32 (1993), arXiv:hep-th/9209099](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9209099)
- [Tom Lada, Martin Markl, Strongly homotopy Lie algebras, Comm. Algebra 23 (1995), arXiv:hep-th/9406095](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-th/9406095)

### Abelian extensions classified by H² make the Levi decomposition a vanishing statement

**Remember:** A Levi factor is a splitting, and H² = 0 provides it.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔰 and module M, H²(𝔰,M) classifies, up to equivalence, extensions of 𝔰 by an abelian ideal M with the given action. The zero class is exactly the split extensions, those with a Lie algebra section of the quotient map (our own).

**Problem.** Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, with radical 𝔯 (its largest solvable ideal). Then 𝔤 = 𝔰 ⋉ 𝔯 for a semisimple subalgebra 𝔰, so 𝔤 = 𝔰 ⊕ 𝔯 as vector spaces (Levi).

**How the definition helps.** Induct on the dimension of the radical, and take the last nonzero term I of its derived series, an abelian ideal of 𝔤 (our own). The preimage in 𝔤 of a Levi factor of 𝔤/I is an extension of a semisimple algebra by I (our own). Whitehead’s second lemma makes its class zero, so it splits and gives a Levi factor of 𝔤 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology), [Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead%27s_lemma_%28Lie_algebra%29). It says: “Similarly, Whitehead's second lemma states that under the conditions of the first lemma, also H²(𝔤,V) = 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cocycles detect split central extensions

**Remember:** The extension splits when a change of section erases the bracket error.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a central extension with kernel Z, pick any linear section s of the quotient map and measure its bracket error c(x,y) = \[s(x),s(y)\] − s(\[x,y\]) in Z. The extension class is c modulo the errors f(\[x,y\]) that come from changing s by a linear map f into Z (our own).

**Problem.** A central extension of Lie algebras over a field splits, meaning some section preserves brackets, exactly when its class in H² of the quotient with coefficients in the kernel is zero.

**How the definition helps.** Changing s to s + f subtracts f(\[x,y\]) from c, because Z brackets to zero with everything (our own). So the class is zero exactly when some section has zero error, that is, preserves brackets (our own). Such a section splits the extension.

**nLab:** [Lie algebra extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+extension). It says: “The condition on μ₂ to be a 2-cocycle is precisely the condition that this formula satisfies the Jacobi identity.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Cohomology turns Weyl’s splitting problem into vanishing

**Remember:** A zero extension class means a splitting that respects the action.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B10, 17B20. arXiv math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a module extension of V by W, pick a linear section s and measure its failure to respect the action, c(x)(v) = x·s(v) − s(x·v). Its class in H¹(𝔤,Hom(V,W)) is c modulo the errors x ↦ x·f from changing s by a linear map f from V to W (our own).

**Problem.** Over a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra in characteristic zero, every finite-dimensional module is a direct sum of irreducible modules. Whitehead’s first lemma gives H¹(𝔤,M) = 0 for every finite-dimensional module M.

**How the definition helps.** If the class is zero, changing s by a suitable f cancels its error (our own). The new section respects the action, so its image is a submodule complementing W (our own). Whitehead’s first lemma makes every class zero, and induction on dimension gives the decomposition (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl%27s_theorem_on_complete_reducibility). It says: “The theorem is an easy consequence of Whitehead's lemma”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Defining cohomology as Ext lets the Casimir kill all cohomology

**Remember:** The Casimir is zero on k and invertible on V, so Ext vanishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B10. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 over k and a module M, Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is Extⁿ over U(𝔤) from the trivial module k to M. So a central element of U(𝔤) acts on it through either argument, with the same result (our own).

**Problem.** Let 𝔤 be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero. If V is a finite-dimensional irreducible module on which 𝔤 acts nontrivially, then Hⁿ(𝔤,V) = 0 for every n.

**How the definition helps.** The Killing-form Casimir is central, acts by zero on k, and acts invertibly on a nontrivial irreducible V under these hypotheses (our own). Acting through k and through V gives the same map on Ext, which is both zero and invertible. So Ext vanishes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Whitehead's lemma (Lie algebra)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitehead%27s_lemma_%28Lie_algebra%29), [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “further let V be irreducible under the 𝔤-action and let 𝔤 act nontrivially, so 𝔤 · V ≠ 0. Then H<sup>q</sup>(𝔤,V) = 0 for all q ≥ 0.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Defining Lie cohomology by exterior forms gives a commutative product

**Remember:** A differential with the product rule passes the wedge product to cohomology.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The trivial-coefficient cochains of 𝔤 are the alternating multilinear forms on 𝔤, multiplied by the wedge product. The Chevalley–Eilenberg differential d, the dual of the bracket extended to all forms, obeys the graded product rule d(α∧β) = dα∧β + (−1)ᵖα∧dβ for α of degree p (our own).

**Problem.** Lie algebra cohomology with trivial coefficients is a graded commutative ring. The product comes from the wedge product of forms.

**How the definition helps.** By the product rule, closed forms multiply to closed forms, and a closed form times an exact form is exact (our own). So the wedge product passes to cohomology and keeps its graded commutativity (our own).

**nLab:** [Chevalley-Eilenberg algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Chevalley-Eilenberg+algebra). It says: “the graded-commutative dg-algebra structures on ∧•𝔤∗ are precisely in bijection with Lie algebra structures on 𝔤”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Derivations modulo inner derivations make Levi factors conjugate

**Remember:** Each layer's difference is a derivation; Whitehead makes it inner.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B05. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** H¹(𝔰,M) is the space of derivations into M, the linear maps f with f(\[x,y\]) = x·f(y) − y·f(x), modulo the inner ones x ↦ x·m for m in M.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic zero, any two Levi subalgebras are conjugate (Malcev). The conjugating automorphism has the form exp(ad z), with z in the nilradical.

**How the definition helps.** Two Levi sections agree modulo the nilradical, and at each lower central layer of the nilradical their difference is a derivation into that abelian layer (our own). Whitehead’s first lemma makes it inner, so conjugating by an exponential from that layer removes it (our own). Nilpotence ends the process, and the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff formula combines the steps into one exp(ad z) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Levi decomposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Levi_decomposition), [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Moreover, Malcev (1942) showed that any two Levi subalgebras are conjugate by an (inner) automorphism of the form exp(ad(z)) where z is in the nilradical (Levi–Malcev theorem).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Derived invariants give the cohomology long exact sequence

**Remember:** Cohomology is derived invariants, and derived functors give long sequences.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G15. arXiv math.RA, math.KT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is the n-th right derived functor of the invariants functor, which sends a module M to the elements m with x·m = 0 for every x in 𝔤. This functor is left exact on U(𝔤)-modules.

**Problem.** A short exact sequence of 𝔤-modules gives a long exact sequence in Lie algebra cohomology.

**How the definition helps.** The right derived functors of any left exact functor turn each short exact sequence into a long exact sequence. Invariants are left exact, so Lie algebra cohomology has this sequence (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Equivalently, these are the right derived functors of the left exact invariant submodule functor”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Invariant forms are cocycles, so the Killing 3-form gives nonzero H³

**Remember:** Invariant forms are closed and never exact on reductive Lie algebras.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B20. arXiv math.RT, math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An alternating form on 𝔤 is invariant when every coadjoint operator θ(x) kills it. Koszul’s formula d = ½ ∑ᵢ eⁱ ∧ θ(eᵢ), for dual bases eᵢ and eⁱ, then makes d zero on every invariant form (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite-dimensional reductive Lie algebra 𝔤 over a characteristic-zero field k, H\*(𝔤;k) is the algebra of invariant alternating forms. For nonzero semisimple 𝔤, the Killing form gives a nonzero class in H³ via (x,y,z) ↦ ⟨x,\[y,z\]⟩, although H¹ and H² vanish.

**How the definition helps.** Koszul’s formula makes every invariant form closed (our own). Complete reducibility of the cochains, with 𝔤 acting trivially on cohomology, identifies invariant forms with all cohomology classes (our own). For nonzero semisimple 𝔤, the Killing form is nondegenerate and \[𝔤,𝔤\] = 𝔤, so the 3-form ⟨x,\[y,z\]⟩ is nonzero (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “For instance for 𝔤 a semisimple Lie algebra, there is the Killing form ⟨−,−⟩. The corresponding 3-cocycle is μ := ⟨−,\[−,−\]⟩ ∈ CE(𝔤)”

**Sources:**

- [J.-L. Koszul, Homologie et cohomologie des algèbres de Lie, Bull. Soc. Math. France 78 (1950) 65–127](https://doi.org/10.24033/bsmf.1410)

### Invariants in two stages give the Hochschild–Serre spectral sequence

**Remember:** Take 𝔥-invariants, then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants, and derive the composite.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 18G40. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is the n-th right derived functor of taking 𝔤-invariants. For an ideal 𝔥 of 𝔤, taking 𝔤-invariants is the same as taking 𝔥-invariants and then 𝔤/𝔥-invariants.

**Problem.** For an ideal 𝔥 of a Lie algebra 𝔤 and a 𝔤-module M, there is a spectral sequence from H\*(𝔤/𝔥; H\*(𝔥;M)) to H\*(𝔤;M). Its low-degree terms give the five-term inflation-restriction exact sequence.

**How the definition helps.** Grothendieck’s spectral sequence for this composite of two functors gives the result (our own). It applies because 𝔥-invariants preserve injectives, being right adjoint to the exact inflation, and restriction to 𝔥 preserves injectives because U(𝔤) is free over U(𝔥) (our own). The five-term sequence comes from the low degrees.

**nLab:** [Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Hochschild-Serre+spectral+sequence). It says: “The invariants can be computed in two stages, hence as the composite of two functors”

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “the inflation-restriction sequence (namely, the 5-term sequence induced by the Hochschild-Serre spectral sequence) associated with the exact sequence of ℕ-graded 𝔽-Lie algebras 0→I→ℱ→ℒ→0”

**Sources:**

- [G. Hochschild and J.-P. Serre, Cohomology of Lie algebras, Ann. of Math. 57 (1953) 591–603](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969740)

### Left-invariant forms make Lie algebra cohomology the cohomology of compact groups

**Remember:** Average forms over a compact group, and only Lie algebra data remain.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T10. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A differential form ω on a Lie group G is left-invariant if Lₐ\*ω = ω for every left translation Lₐ. Evaluation at the identity turns these forms into the alternating forms on 𝔤, and the de Rham differential into the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential (our own).

**Problem.** For a compact connected Lie group G, the de Rham cohomology of G is isomorphic to the Lie algebra cohomology H\*(𝔤;ℝ). This fails without compactness: the group ℝ is contractible, but H¹ of its Lie algebra is ℝ.

**How the definition helps.** So left-invariant forms compute H\*(𝔤;ℝ). For compact G, Haar averaging projects all forms onto left-invariant forms and commutes with the differential. For connected G each translation is homotopic to the identity, so averaging does not change cohomology classes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_cohomology). It says: “Using an averaging process, this complex can be replaced by the complex of left-invariant differential forms.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### Relative cochains are invariant forms, so relative cohomology computes compact homogeneous spaces

**Remember:** Invariant forms on G/K are exactly the relative cochains.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 57T15. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 with subalgebra 𝔨, the relative cochains are the 𝔨-invariant alternating forms on 𝔤/𝔨 with the Chevalley–Eilenberg differential. For connected K, these are exactly the values at the base point of G-invariant forms on G/K (our own).

**Problem.** Let G be a compact connected Lie group and K a closed connected subgroup. Then the de Rham cohomology of G/K is isomorphic to H\*(𝔤,𝔨;ℝ).

**How the definition helps.** At the base point a G-invariant form on G/K is a K-invariant alternating form on 𝔤/𝔨, which for connected K means 𝔨-invariant, and the differentials agree (our own). Averaging over compact connected G shows that invariant forms compute de Rham cohomology (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “consisting of the 𝔥-invariant elements in the tensor product of V with the exterior algebra of the coset 𝔤/𝔥.”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### The Chevalley–Eilenberg resolution makes cohomology vanish above the dimension

**Remember:** No alternating forms above dim 𝔤, so no cohomology there.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B35. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The degree-n Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains of 𝔤 with values in M are the alternating n-linear maps from 𝔤 to M, that is, maps from Λⁿ𝔤. They come from a resolution of k by the modules U(𝔤) ⊗ Λⁿ𝔤, which stops at n = dim 𝔤.

**Problem.** For a Lie algebra 𝔤 of finite dimension d over a field, Hⁿ(𝔤,M) = 0 for every module M and every n &gt; d. Hence Ext over U(𝔤) between any two modules vanishes above degree d, so U(𝔤) has global dimension at most d.

**How the definition helps.** Λⁿ𝔤 = 0 for n &gt; d, so there are no cochains, hence no cohomology, above d (our own). For modules N and M, Ext from N to M over U(𝔤) is Lie cohomology with coefficients in Homₖ(N,M), so the same bound holds (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “Lie algebra cohomology and homology were defined by Chevalley-Eilenberg with a help of concrete Koszul-type resolution”

**Sources:**

- [C. Chevalley and S. Eilenberg, Cohomology theory of Lie groups and Lie algebras, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 63 (1948) 85–124](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9947-1948-0024908-8)

### The Ext definition gives free Lie algebras cohomological dimension one

**Remember:** A two-term resolution of tensor algebras stops free Lie cohomology at H¹.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B01. arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hⁿ(𝔤,M) is Extⁿ over U(𝔤) from the trivial module to M. For the free Lie algebra on V, U is the tensor algebra T(V), whose augmentation ideal is the free module T(V) ⊗ V, so the trivial module has a resolution of length one.

**Problem.** If 𝔣 is a free Lie algebra, then Hⁿ(𝔣,M) = 0 for every module M and every n ≥ 2. Conversely, an ℕ-graded Lie algebra L generated by its degree-one part with H²(L,𝔽) = 0 is free.

**How the definition helps.** The resolution 0 → T(V) ⊗ V → T(V) → k → 0 gives Hⁿ = 0 for n ≥ 2. Conversely, write L = F/R with F free on L₁, so R starts in degree two; inflation-restriction and H²(L,𝔽) = 0 give R = \[F,R\], since F and L have the same abelianization (our own). A nonzero R would have a lowest degree outside \[F,R\], so R = 0 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034). It says: “If ℒ is free, then H²(ℒ,𝔽)=0, since 0→𝒰(ℒ)⊗ℒ₁→𝒰(ℒ)→𝔽→0 is a projective resolution of the trivial 𝒰(ℒ)-module 𝔽.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurosh theorem for certain Koszul Lie algebras, arXiv:2201.03034](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.03034)

### The symmetric-space involution kills the differential on invariant forms

**Remember:** The involution has sign (−1)ᵏ, so d must be zero.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 53C35, 57T15. arXiv math.RT, math.DG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A compact symmetric space G/K has an involution σ of G whose fixed group contains K as an open subgroup. At the base point σ acts as −1 on the tangent space 𝔭, where G-invariant forms are the K-invariant alternating forms on 𝔭 (our own).

**Problem.** Let G/K be a compact symmetric space with G compact and connected. Then every G-invariant differential form on G/K is closed, so the de Rham cohomology of G/K is (Λ𝔭\*)ᴷ, the K-invariant forms on 𝔭 (Cartan).

**How the definition helps.** So σ acts by (−1)ᵏ on invariant k-forms and by (−1)ᵏ⁺¹ on their differentials (our own). Since σ commutes with d, every invariant form ω has dω = 0 (our own). Averaging over compact connected G shows that invariant forms compute de Rham cohomology (our own).

**nLab:** [Lie algebra cohomology](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Lie+algebra+cohomology). It says: “consisting of the 𝔥-invariant elements in the tensor product of V with the exterior algebra of the coset 𝔤/𝔥.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Universal central extensions exist exactly for perfect Lie algebras, with kernel H₂

**Remember:** A universal central extension lifts uniquely into every central extension.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B56 (Cohomology of Lie (super)algebras), 17B55. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A central extension of 𝔤 is a surjection 𝔢 → 𝔤 whose kernel lies in the center of 𝔢. A universal central extension is one with a unique map to every other central extension of 𝔤, and 𝔤 is perfect when \[𝔤,𝔤\] = 𝔤.

**Problem.** A Lie algebra 𝔤 over a field has a universal central extension if and only if 𝔤 is perfect. Then the extension is unique up to unique isomorphism, and its kernel is the homology H₂(𝔤).

**How the definition helps.** If 𝔤 is not perfect, a nonzero linear form vanishing on \[𝔤,𝔤\] gives two different maps into a split central extension, so none is universal (our own). If 𝔤 is perfect, Λ²𝔤 modulo boundaries from Λ³𝔤, mapped to 𝔤 by the bracket, is universal: it is perfect, and bracketing lifts gives the maps (our own). Its kernel is cycles modulo boundaries, H₂(𝔤), and initiality gives uniqueness up to unique isomorphism (our own).

**nLab:** [universal central extension](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/universal+central+extension). It says: “the universal central extension is, if it exists, the initial object in the category of central extensions of that object.”

**Wikipedia:** [Lie algebra extension](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie_algebra_extension). It says: “By universality, it is easy to conclude that such universal central extensions are unique up to isomorphism.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Witt brackets inherit Jacobi

**Remember:** Use commutators of operators and Jacobi comes from composition.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B66 (Lie algebras of vector fields and related (super) algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The complex Witt algebra is the space of complex-linear derivations of ℂ\[z,z⁻¹\], the maps D with D(fg) = D(f)g + fD(g), with the commutator DE − ED of operators as bracket.

**Problem.** The bracket on the complex Witt algebra obeys the Jacobi identity.

**How the definition helps.** For commutators in an associative algebra of operators, the Jacobi sum expands into terms that cancel in pairs (our own). It remains only to check that a commutator of derivations is again a derivation (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Witt algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witt_algebra). It says: “the Lie algebra of derivations of the ring C\[z,z⁻¹\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Realizations of singular Cartan matrices keep simple roots linearly independent

**Remember:** Enlarge the space 𝔥 until the simple roots stop colliding.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B67 (Kac-Moody (super)algebras; extended affine Lie algebras; toroidal Lie algebras), 17B22. arXiv math.RA, math.RT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A realization of an n×n generalized Cartan matrix C of rank r is a complex space 𝔥 of dimension 2n − r with independent vectors h₁,…,hₙ and independent covectors α₁,…,αₙ satisfying αⱼ(hᵢ) = cᵢⱼ. The extra n − r dimensions keep the simple roots independent even when C is singular.

**Problem.** Every generalized Cartan matrix has a realization, unique up to isomorphism. The Kac–Moody algebra it defines splits into 𝔥 and root spaces, and every root is an integer combination of simple roots with coefficients all of one sign.

**How the definition helps.** Dimension 2n − r is enough for n independent coroots and n independent roots with these pairings, and extending bases gives existence and uniqueness (our own). Independent simple roots give every root a well-defined degree. The Kac–Moody triangular decomposition then gives the root spaces and the sign rule (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kac–Moody algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kac%E2%80%93Moody_algebra). It says: “The vector space 𝔥 has dimension 2n − r … The sets {αᵢ} and {αᵢ∨} are linearly independent”

**Sources:**

- [Moody, R. V. (1967). Lie algebras associated with generalized Cartan matrices. Bulletin of the AMS 73, 217–222.](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1967-11688-4)
- [Kac, V. G. (1968). Simple irreducible graded Lie algebras of finite growth. Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya 2.](https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1968v002n06ABEH000729)

### Locality and translation give skew symmetry

**Remember:** Fields commute up to poles, and T slides the insertion point.

*True by definition.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a vertex algebra, locality says each pair of fields commutes up to a pole: (z − w)ᴺ\[Y(u,z),Y(v,w)\] = 0 for some N ≥ 0. Translation says \[T,Y(u,z)\] = ∂Y(u,z)/∂z with T1 = 0, and creation says Y(u,z)1 has no negative powers and constant term u.

**Problem.** For all states u,v in a complex vertex algebra, skew symmetry gives Y(u,z)v = exp(zT)Y(v,−z)u.

**How the definition helps.** Apply locality to the vacuum and use Y(a,w)1 = exp(wT)a (our own). Translation covariance rewrites the reversed product as exp(zT)Y(v,w − z)u (our own). After clearing poles, set w = 0 and cancel the common power of z (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Vertex operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_operator_algebra). It says: “(skew-symmetry) Y(u,z)v=eᶻᵀY(v,−z)u”

**Sources:**

- [Frenkel and Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)

### One character forces modular invariance

**Remember:** One module, one character, so the modular group acts by a scalar.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A holomorphic vertex operator algebra is a simple, rational, self-dual, C₂-cofinite vertex operator algebra V of CFT type whose only simple module, up to isomorphism, is V itself. So it has a single character, q<sup>(−c/24)</sup> ∑ₙ dim(Vₙ)qⁿ with q = exp(2πiτ) and c the central charge.

**Problem.** If a holomorphic vertex operator algebra has central charge divisible by 24, its character is invariant under the modular group.

**How the definition helps.** Zhu’s theorem makes the span of simple characters a modular representation, and here that span is one-dimensional, so each element acts by a scalar. Translation τ ↦ τ+1 multiplies the character by exp(−2πic/24), which is 1 when 24 divides c but not for the E₈ lattice algebra with c = 8 (our own). In the abelian image, S² = (ST)³ gives S = T⁻³, so inversion also acts trivially (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3), [Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3). It says: “Then 𝔠𝔥\[V\] is a right Γ-submodule of 𝔉.”

**Sources:**

- [Cameron Franc, Geoffrey Mason, Character Vectors of Strongly Regular Vertex Operator Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04616v3)
- [Yongchang Zhu, Modular invariance of characters of vertex operator algebras](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0894-0347-96-00182-8)
- [Chongying Dong, Vertex Algebras Associated with Even Lattices](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1993.1217)

### Truncation excludes evaluation modules

**Remember:** High modes kill each vector, so every current is a field.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures). arXiv math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Over the centrally extended loop algebra of a finite-dimensional complex simple Lie algebra with a fixed invariant form, a module has level k if the central element acts by k. It is restricted if, for each current x and each vector w, the modes x⊗tⁿ kill w for all large n, which says exactly that each current series ∑ₙ (x⊗tⁿ)z<sup>(−n−1)</sup> is a field (our own).

**Problem.** At level k, restriction to current modes identifies modules of the universal affine vertex algebra with restricted level-k modules of the centrally extended loop algebra.

**How the definition helps.** A module of the universal affine vertex algebra is a space where every current acts as a field, and restrictedness says exactly that (our own). Affine reconstruction then extends each restricted level-k action uniquely to the whole vertex algebra (our own). An evaluation module at t = 1 fails, because a nonzero current repeats the same operator at every mode, so no mode kills w (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A unified construction of vertex algebras from infinite-dimensional Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16744v1). It says: “Γσ-equivariant φε-coordinated quasi Vℒ̂(𝔟)-modules are exactly restricted ℒ̂(𝔟,σ)-modules.”

**Sources:**

- [Fulin Chen, Xiaoling Liao, Shaobin Tan, Qing Wang, A unified construction of vertex algebras from infinite-dimensional Lie algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16744v1)
- [Edward Frenkel and David Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)

### Unimodularity removes extra modules

**Remember:** Lattice equals its dual, so one coset, so one module.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17B69 (Vertex operators; vertex operator algebras and related structures), 81T40. arXiv math.QA, math-ph. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An even positive definite lattice L is unimodular if it equals its dual, the vectors in its real span that pair integrally with all of L. Equivalently, the quotient of the dual by L, which indexes the simple modules of the lattice vertex algebra, is trivial (our own).

**Problem.** An even positive definite lattice gives a holomorphic vertex operator algebra exactly when it is unimodular. Here holomorphic means that the vacuum module is the only simple module with finite-dimensional weight spaces and weights bounded below.

**How the definition helps.** Dong’s classification gives one simple module for each coset of L in its dual, with L itself giving the vacuum module (our own). So the vacuum module is the only one exactly when that quotient is trivial (our own). For L = ℤα with α² = 2, the vector α/2 lies in the dual and gives a second module (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Vertex operator algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertex_operator_algebra). It says: “Lattice vertex algebras are canonically attached to double covers of even integral lattices”

**Sources:**

- [Frenkel and Ben-Zvi, Vertex Algebras and Algebraic Curves](https://doi.org/10.1090/surv/088)
- [Chongying Dong, Vertex Algebras Associated with Even Lattices](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1993.1217)

### Parity signs give the supercommutator its Jacobi identity

**Remember:** Two odd inputs turn the commutator into an anticommutator.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 17B70 (Graded Lie (super)algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In an associative algebra graded modulo two, the supercommutator of homogeneous x and y of parities i and j is \[x,y\] = xy − (−1)ⁱʲyx, extended bilinearly. The sign makes the bracket of two odd elements the anticommutator xy + yx, which is symmetric, as a Lie superalgebra requires (our own).

**Problem.** Over a field of characteristic zero, the supercommutator defines a Lie superalgebra on any associative algebra graded by parity.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding the signed Jacobi identity with associativity, each product of three factors appears twice with opposite signs, so the sum is zero (our own). The ordinary commutator fails: in 2×2 matrices with off-diagonal matrices odd, \[E₁₂,E₂₁\] = E₁₁ − E₂₂ is nonzero and changes sign under exchange, but odd inputs need a symmetric bracket (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Superalgebras with Homogeneous structures of Lie type](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00618). It says: “Any Super-associative superalgebra is a Super-Lie admissible superalgebra.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Jacobi sum kills cubes

**Remember:** The Jacobi sum is the mixed part of a cube.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C05 (Identities and free Jordan structures). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A commutative algebra is Jacobi–Jordan if its Jacobi sum vanishes: (xy)z + (yz)x + (zx)y = 0 for all x,y,z. With all three inputs equal the sum is 3x³, and in general it is half the fully mixed part of the cube (x+y+z)³ (our own).

**Problem.** For a commutative algebra over a field of characteristic other than two or three, the Jacobi identity holds exactly when all cubes vanish.

**How the definition helps.** Setting all inputs equal gives 3x³ = 0, and 3 is invertible (our own). Conversely, (x+y+z)³ − (x+y)³ − (y+z)³ − (z+x)³ + x³ + y³ + z³ equals twice the Jacobi sum, and 2 is invertible (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology and deformations of Jacobi-Jordan algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12364v1). It says: “such that x³ = 0, ∀ x ∈ J.”

**Sources:**

- [Amir Baklouti, Said Benayadi, Abdenacer Makhlouf, Sabeur Mansour. Cohomology and deformations of Jacobi-Jordan algebras, Proposition 2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.12364v1)
- [Dietrich Burde and Alice Fialowski. Jacobi–Jordan algebras (2014).](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.laa.2014.07.034)

### Quadratic operators produce inner ideals

**Remember:** Sandwich by a sandwich, and Q(a) stays the outer bread.

*True by definition.* MSC 17C10 (Structure theory for Jordan algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a quadratic Jordan algebra J, a subspace B is an inner ideal if the sandwich Q(b)c lies in B for every b ∈ B and c ∈ J. The fundamental formula Q(Q(a)b) = Q(a)Q(b)Q(a) says that sandwiching by an element of the image of Q(a) applies Q(a) last.

**Problem.** For every a in a quadratic Jordan algebra, the image of Q(a) is an inner ideal.

**How the definition helps.** For b′ = Q(a)b, the formula gives Q(b′)c = Q(a)(Q(b)Q(a)c), which lies in the image of Q(a) (our own). Starting from a binary Jordan product, one would first have to prove the fundamental formula (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic Jordan algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_Jordan_algebra). It says: “For given b, the image of Q(b) is an inner ideal”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Alternating associators force flexibility

**Remember:** Any repeated input kills the associator, including the outer two.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebra is alternative if its associator (x,y,z) = (xy)z − x(yz) is alternating, meaning it vanishes whenever two of its three inputs are equal. The usual left and right laws, (x,x,y) = 0 and (y,x,x) = 0, already give this.

**Problem.** Every alternative algebra satisfies (xy)x = x(yx), even in characteristic two.

**How the definition helps.** Flexibility (xy)x = x(yx) is the case (x,y,x) = 0 of equal first and third inputs. From the two laws, linearizing the right law gives (x,y,x) = −(x,x,y), which the left law makes zero, with no division by 2 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “By definition, a multilinear map is alternating if it vanishes whenever two of its arguments are equal.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Artin’s theorem reverses unit products

**Remember:** Put two units in one associative algebra, then reverse their order.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A unital algebra is alternative if any two elements generate an associative subalgebra. By Artin’s theorem, this is equivalent to x(xy) = (xx)y and (yx)x = y(xx) for all x,y (our own). A unit is an element with a two-sided inverse.

**Problem.** In a finite-dimensional unital alternative algebra over a field, a product of two units is a unit. Its inverse is the product of their inverses in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** Inside the associative subalgebra generated by units u, v and 1, the inverse of uv is v⁻¹u⁻¹, provided u⁻¹ and v⁻¹ lie there (our own). Finite dimension gives this: left multiplication by u is injective on the subalgebra generated by u and 1, hence onto, and the element w there with uw = 1 equals u⁻¹ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Alternative algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alternative_algebra). It says: “If x and y are invertible then xy is also invertible with inverse (xy)⁻¹ = y⁻¹x⁻¹.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Commutative alternative algebras associate without three-torsion

**Remember:** Three times the associator vanishes, so rule out three-torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 17D05 (Alternative rings). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebra is alternative if its associator (x,y,z) = (xy)z − x(yz) vanishes whenever two inputs agree, so it changes sign under any swap of two inputs. Its additive group has no three-torsion if 3a = 0 forces a = 0.

**Problem.** A commutative alternative algebra without additive three-torsion is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Commutativity makes the cyclic sum (x,y,z) + (y,z,x) + (z,x,y) vanish, and alternation makes its three terms equal, so 3(x,y,z) = 0 and without three-torsion every associator vanishes (our own). In characteristic three, take the commutative algebra with basis x,y,z,u,v,w,t and nonzero products xy = u, yz = v, zx = w, uz = t, wy = −t (our own). It is alternative, yet (x,y,z) = t (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426). It says: “For each a,b,c ∈ K, we have 3((ab)c − a(bc)) = 0. Hence, K is associative if K has no 3-torsion.”

**Sources:**

- [Cubic norm pairs and hermitian cubic norm structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.10426)

### Pre-Lie left multiplication preserves brackets

**Remember:** Left multiplication takes each bracket to the bracket of operators.

*True by definition.* MSC 17D25 (Lie-admissible algebras). arXiv math.RA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a bilinear product on a vector space, let L(x) be left multiplication z ↦ xz. The product is left pre-Lie if \[L(x),L(y)\] = L(xy − yx) for all x,y, so left multiplication turns the commutator bracket into the operator commutator.

**Problem.** In a left pre-Lie algebra, the bracket \[x,y\] = xy − yx makes the algebra a Lie algebra. Left multiplication represents it by linear operators whose commutator equals L(\[x,y\]).

**How the definition helps.** The defining equation is exactly the claim that L preserves brackets. Applied to z, it says (x,y,z) = (y,x,z) for the associator (a,b,c) = (ab)c − a(bc) (our own). Expanding the Jacobi sum of xy − yx gives associators that this symmetry cancels in pairs.

**Paper or page:** [Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5). It says: “Furthermore, the map adᴸ: L → gl(L) with x ↦ Lₓ gives a representation of the Lie algebra (L,\[·,·\]).”

**Sources:**

- [A. Ben Hassine, T. Chtioui, M. Elhamdadi, S. Mabrouk. Cohomology and Deformations of left-symmetric Rinehart Algebras, Lemma 2.2.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.00335v5)

### Dendriform sums are associative

**Remember:** Split the product in two; the three laws add to associativity.

*True by definition.* MSC 17A30 (Nonassociative algebras satisfying other identities). arXiv math.RA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A dendriform dialgebra splits a product x ∗ y = x ≺ y + x ≻ y into two bilinear products with three laws: (x≺y)≺z = x≺(y∗z), (x≻y)≺z = x≻(y≺z) and (x∗y)≻z = x≻(y≻z). The three left sides add up to (x∗y)∗z and the three right sides to x∗(y∗z) (our own).

**Problem.** The sum of the two dendriform operations is associative.

**How the definition helps.** Adding the three laws gives (x∗y)∗z = x∗(y∗z) directly (our own).

**nLab:** [dendriform algebra](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/dendriform+algebra). It says: “The sum of the two binary operations is an associative operation.”

**Sources:**

- [Jean-Louis Loday. Dialgebras (2001).](https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-45328-8_2)
